# Conti Ransomware Leaks and Public Attribution Record

## Executive Summary

Public sources describe Conti as a large, professionally organized ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation associated with the broader Wizard Spider cybercrime ecosystem. The available evidence supports a distinction between three types of information: government assessments and reward allegations, independent technical and threat-intelligence reporting, and criminal-case allegations or adjudicated developments.

The strongest common conclusion is that Conti operated through a commercialized model in which malware developers and organizational managers supported affiliates or operators who conducted intrusions. Conti generally used double extortion: operators stole data, encrypted victims’ systems, demanded payment, and threatened to publish or sell the stolen information if victims did not pay. The U.S. Department of State’s Rewards for Justice program assesses that Conti, also known as Wizard Spider, was a Russian government-linked RaaS group that targeted U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. It identifies the online aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” as malicious cyber actors believed to be linked to Conti. These are government reward-program allegations and assessments, not judicial findings in the sources provided. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

The ContiLeaks disclosures materially strengthened public understanding of the group’s internal organization. The leaked communications reportedly included 393 JSON files totaling approximately 14 megabytes, internal discussions, screenshots, operational details, and conversations concerning staffing, salaries, product development, security testing, infrastructure, and financial matters. Rapid7 reported that the communications made Conti appear more like a software company than a loose criminal collective, with technical interviews, coding exercises, salary negotiations, and specialized personnel. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

The Center for Internet Security similarly describes Conti as a commercially structured RaaS enterprise with distinct functional units, including coders, testers, administrators, reverse engineers, and penetration testers or hackers. It reports that an insider claimed the operation employed more than 60 people in July 2021, although staffing fluctuated. ([S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

Separately, a U.S. Department of Justice case page identifies Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, and Oleksii Lytvynenko in Conti-related criminal proceedings. The page states that the first four defendants were charged with conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. It states that Lytvynenko was charged in connection with a conspiracy to deploy Conti ransomware and later entered a guilty plea to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The page expressly preserves the presumption of innocence for defendants who have not been convicted. ([S4](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

The evidence therefore supports a concrete conclusion: Conti was publicly documented as a scalable, specialized, and commercially managed RaaS organization; the 2022 leaks exposed how that structure worked in practice; and later law-enforcement records connected named defendants to Conti-related conspiracies, while the supplied sources do not establish that any of those defendants used the aliases listed in the Rewards for Justice notice.

## Scope and Source Reliability

This report uses only the four distinct source records supplied in the benchmark material:

| Source ID | Publisher | Principal evidentiary role |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | U.S. Department of State, Rewards for Justice | Government reward notice, attribution assessment, aliases, alleged targeting and activity |
| S2 | Rapid7 | Independent threat-intelligence analysis of the ContiLeaks disclosures |
| S3 | Center for Internet Security | Analysis of Conti’s commercialization and RaaS structure |
| S4 | U.S. Department of Justice, Middle District of Tennessee | Official criminal-case information, charges, plea, and procedural status |

The sources should not be treated as interchangeable. S1 contains official government assessments and allegations made for a reward program. S2 and S3 analyze leaked material and public reporting but are not court findings. S4 is an official law-enforcement record and is the most authoritative source for the procedural status of the named defendants. However, an indictment or charge is an allegation unless resolved by a conviction or guilty plea.

## How Public Sources Describe Conti as an RaaS Operation

### Commercial model and division of labor

The RaaS model described in the supplied sources separates the development and administration of ransomware from the execution of individual intrusions. CIS explains that RaaS groups lease or provide malware to affiliates, who conduct intrusions and share proceeds with the developers. The source describes a common revenue arrangement as approximately a 70–30 split, while emphasizing that the exact structure can vary. ([S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

This model enabled specialization. Instead of requiring one group to perform every stage of an intrusion, different participants could focus on malware development, access acquisition, phishing, exploitation, negotiation, or data theft. CIS specifically explains that initial access brokers could sell already established access to victim environments. This allowed ransomware affiliates to begin operations more quickly and allowed the RaaS operator to scale without personally conducting every intrusion. ([S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

Rapid7’s review of the leaked chats presents a similar picture. It reports that Conti’s internal communications covered interviews, technical coding exercises, salary negotiations, product status, payments for services, and routine workplace matters. Those details are significant because they show that Conti’s organizational practices resembled those of a conventional software enterprise, even though its product and activities were criminal. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

### Double extortion and operational workflow

The public descriptions identify Conti as a double-extortion operation. According to CIS, Conti stole victims’ data and encrypted systems, then used the threat of publication to pressure victims to pay. ([S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization/))

The Rewards for Justice notice describes a similar workflow: Conti operators typically stole files and encrypted servers and workstations; ransom instructions directed victims to an online portal; and failure to pay could result in stolen data being sold or published on a site controlled by the operators. The notice states that some ransom demands reached as high as $25 million. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

The DOJ’s case page provides a narrower description, stating that Conti ransomware infected computers and networks and encrypted victims’ data. The page does not independently describe every stage of the double-extortion process, but it is consistent with the broader operational description in S1 and S3. ([S4](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

### Scale and victim profile

The supplied sources report different figures that appear to measure different aspects of Conti’s activity. The Rewards for Justice notice states that Conti ransomware was used in more than 1,000 ransomware operations targeting U.S. and international critical infrastructure. It also states that more than 400 organizations worldwide were victimized, including more than 290 in the United States. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

The DOJ case page states that Conti affected more than 900 businesses, nonprofits, governments, and other victims in the United States and around the world. ([S4](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

These figures should not be automatically combined. “Operations,” “organizations,” and “victims” may refer to different counting methods or reporting periods. The sources do not provide enough methodological detail to reconcile them precisely. The appropriate conclusion is that all supplied government descriptions portray Conti as a high-volume operation affecting hundreds of organizations and, depending on the metric, more than 900 victims or more than 1,000 operations.

The victim categories identified in S1 included law-enforcement agencies, emergency medical services, 9-1-1 dispatch centers, municipalities, healthcare networks, and other critical infrastructure. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/)) CIS adds that reported Conti-related attacks affecting state, local, tribal, and territorial entities included municipal governments and education facilities. It reports 22 Conti-related SLTT attacks received by MS-ISAC from mid-2020 through January 2022. ([S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

## What the Leaks Exposed About Conti’s Internal Structure

### The ContiLeaks disclosure

Rapid7 reports that, beginning on February 27, 2022, the account known as “@ContiLeaks” released a large archive of internal Conti chat logs after Conti publicly expressed support for the Russian government following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The archive reportedly contained 14 megabytes of chat logs across 393 JSON files. Some messages were encrypted and unreadable, making the available record incomplete. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

The leak also reportedly included screenshots of tools, discussions of exploits and development processes, usernames and passwords, alleged server access details, and a purported ransomware source-code file. Rapid7 states that it did not access remote systems using the exposed credentials and recommended against doing so. That caution is important: the existence of leaked credentials or infrastructure details in a public report is not itself proof that every item was authentic or operational. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

### Functional departments

CIS reports that the leaked material revealed distinct business units and personnel categories. These included:

- **Coders**, who wrote malicious code and integrated technologies;
- **Testers**, who assessed how ransomware performed against security products;
- **Administrators**;
- **Reverse engineers**; and
- **Penetration testers or hackers**.

CIS also reports that spamming functions were contracted outside the organization and that each department had a budget, although units could borrow money from one another. An alleged insider stated that Conti employed more than 60 people, primarily coders and testers, in July 2021. CIS qualifies this figure by noting that staffing changed and that personnel could be dismissed after security breaches. ([S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

This evidence supports the characterization of Conti as an organized enterprise with internal specialization rather than a single undifferentiated criminal team. It does not, however, establish that every person appearing in the chats was a full-time employee, that all departments existed continuously, or that all named chat participants were personally identified.

### Product development and quality assurance

Rapid7 reports that Conti’s communications discussed technical product requirements, including difficulties encrypting very large files and the development of features for particular targets. The group also attempted to obtain demonstrations of endpoint-detection products to improve its ability to evade security controls. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

CIS provides examples of the group’s investment in operational capability. It reports that Conti allocated $60,000 to acquire a valid license for Cobalt Strike, budgeted several thousand dollars per month for security and antivirus software used in testing, and redirected reverse-engineering efforts toward Windows 11 in July 2021. ([S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

These details are particularly probative of commercialization because they show recurring expenditure on development, testing, and evasion rather than one-off use of an improvised malware tool. They also indicate that Conti treated ransomware as a product requiring compatibility work, testing, and continual improvement.

### Access, phishing, and exploitation

Rapid7 identifies phishing as a common initial-access method and reports that leaked actors shared phishing templates designed to target potential victims. The article also discusses third-party providers for malicious documents and logistics for delivering ransomware without detection by dynamic analysis. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

Rapid7 lists vulnerabilities associated with Conti activity, including MS17-010 vulnerabilities, ZeroLogon, PrintNightmare, Log4Shell, and ProxyShell or ProxyLogon-related vulnerabilities. The presence of these vulnerabilities in the article’s appendix supports a public assessment that Conti exploited known vulnerabilities, but the supplied material does not establish that every listed vulnerability was used in every intrusion. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

## Attribution, Aliases, and Law-Enforcement Records

### Government attribution and aliases

Rewards for Justice states that Conti was also known as Wizard Spider and describes it as a Russian government-linked RaaS group. It further states that the actors known online as “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” were believed to be linked to Conti. The notice associates those aliases with Russia, Conti or Wizard Spider, and applications or tools including Conti ransomware-as-a-service, TrickBot, IcedID, Cobalt Strike, and ZLoader. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

The wording matters. “Believed to be linked” is an attribution assessment, not a criminal conviction or a definitive public identification of a legal name. The supplied source does not provide real-world names for those five aliases, nor does it expressly state that any of them corresponds to Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, or Oleksii Lytvynenko.

The same notice offers a reward of up to $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of persons who, while acting at the direction or under the control of a foreign government, participate in malicious cyber activity against U.S. critical infrastructure in violation of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. This is the legal and policy basis stated for the reward; it should not be read as a judicial determination that each listed alias satisfied those conditions. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

### Defendants and charges

The DOJ’s Middle District of Tennessee page identifies two case numbers. Case 3:23-CR-00092 names Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, and Andrey Zhuykov. Case 3:23-CR-00088 names Oleksii Lytvynenko. ([S4](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

According to the page, on September 7, 2023, the first four defendants were charged with conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The page states that all defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. ([S4](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

The page separately states that Lytvynenko was charged with conspiracy to deploy Conti, a ransomware variant that infected victim computers and networks and encrypted their data. On June 10, 2026, it states that Lytvynenko pleaded guilty to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, pursuant to a plea agreement. ([S4](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

The official record therefore provides a direct law-enforcement link between the named defendants and Conti-related criminal allegations, and an adjudicated plea link for Lytvynenko on the specified wire-fraud count. It does not, in the supplied material, establish convictions for the other defendants, identify them by the aliases in S1, or specify the precise conduct attributable to each individual beyond the charges described.

## Timeline of the Public Record

| Date or period | Event or evidence | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 2019 | S1 says Conti ransomware was first detected | Beginning of the period described by the government notice |
| Mid-2020–January 2022 | MS-ISAC reportedly received 22 Conti-related SLTT attack reports | Evidence of repeated impact on public-sector entities ([S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)) |
| July 2021 | An alleged insider reportedly described more than 60 Conti personnel | Evidence of scale, but based on insider reporting and subject to fluctuation ([S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)) |
| February 24, 2022 | Russia invaded Ukraine | Context for Conti’s political statement and subsequent internal conflict ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)) |
| February 27, 2022 | @ContiLeaks released the first major chat archive | Public exposure of internal communications ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)) |
| March 2–9, 2022 | Rapid7 reported infrastructure takedowns followed by resumed normal operations | Shows disruption but not immediate disappearance ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)) |
| May–June 2022 | CIS reports that the larger Conti platform dismantled, rebranded into smaller units, and later shut down leak and negotiation infrastructure | Indicates organizational fragmentation rather than a simple end to all personnel or activity ([S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)) |
| September 7, 2023 | Four defendants charged in Tennessee | Formal law-enforcement attribution record ([S4](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2)) |
| June 10, 2026 | Lytvynenko pleaded guilty to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud | Adjudicated development in one defendant’s case ([S4](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2)) |

## Contradictions and Uncertainties

Several apparent tensions exist in the supplied material:

1. **Scale figures differ.** S1 reports more than 1,000 operations, more than 400 organizations worldwide, and more than 290 U.S. organizations. S4 reports more than 900 affected victims. These figures are not necessarily contradictory because they may count operations, organizations, and victims differently. The sources do not provide enough methodology to reconcile them.

2. **Operational continuity versus shutdown.** Rapid7 reported that Conti resumed normal operations by March 9, 2022, while CIS later reported that the larger Conti platform shut down and rebranded into smaller units. The most coherent reading is that the exposed central platform experienced disruption and later fragmentation; the evidence does not support the simplistic conclusion that all Conti-linked activity ended immediately after the leak.

3. **Russian government linkage.** S1 characterizes Conti as Russian government-linked. S2 reports that a leaked conversation indicated FSB involvement in some funding and interest in Bellingcat material concerning Navalny. The latter is an interpretation of a conversation, not proof in the supplied sources of a formal command relationship or state sponsorship of every Conti operation.

4. **Aliases and defendants are not cross-matched.** S1 lists five online aliases, while S4 lists five named defendants. No supplied source explicitly maps an alias to a defendant. Any such identification would be speculative and is excluded from this report.

## Conclusion

The evidence supports the conclusion that Conti was not merely a ransomware strain but a mature criminal service ecosystem. Its public profile combines a double-extortion malware operation, affiliate-enabled scaling, specialized internal departments, dedicated testing and development resources, and a victim base extending across government, healthcare, emergency services, education, and other critical infrastructure.

The ContiLeaks disclosures are especially important because they exposed the organization’s internal mechanics: recruiting, coding, testing, budgeting, purchasing tools, managing infrastructure, and improving malware against security products. Those details corroborate the RaaS description independently of the government reward notice.

The attribution record is layered. Rewards for Justice publicly associates Conti/Wizard Spider with Russia and lists the aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis,” but presents those links as government assessments. The DOJ record separately links named defendants to Conti-related conspiracies through charges and, in Lytvynenko’s case, a guilty plea to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The supplied evidence does not establish that the aliases and defendants are the same people. A careful assessment must therefore retain the distinction between intelligence attribution, public reporting, criminal allegations, and adjudicated facts.
